processes.description: A round starts when logistics, volume management or a pipeline group asks for a meter or point record to be created or changed: new points and combinations, a zone re-mapped to a different offer point, a pipe code changed, meters dropped from the estimate file, confirmed noms zeroed, or state and county data corrected. The facilities or scheduling contact makes the change in Global Facilities or the scheduling system and confirms back what was set up and what stays the same, such as the meter number.
steps: A requester sends the meter or point details and the change needed: new set-up, zone re-map, pipe code, estimate list or noms.
The facilities contact checks the existing record and any attached list of meters.
The record is created or changed in Global Facilities or the scheduling system.
Data discrepancies such as wrong state or county information are passed to the group that owns the record.
The person making the change confirms what was set up or changed and what stays the same.

stalls.summary: A forwarded notice of state and county discrepancies on a spreadsheet of meters left the recipient unsure what to do with it, so the correction had no clear owner.

automation.approach: A standard set-up and change request form with required fields for meter, point, pipe code, zone, state and county and effective date, checked against the facilities master before the change is keyed, so mismatches are flagged up front and a confirmation goes back to the requester from the same record.
automation.rationale: Requests arrive in free form from several groups, and the discrepancy notice shows bad location data reaching the records. A form with required fields and a lookup against existing records cuts re-keying and catches errors early, while the facilities team still makes and approves each change.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round is a record change in the facilities or scheduling system: looking up the meter, keying a new point, zone mapping or pipe code, or removing meters from the estimate file, then checking the result. A single change takes about 10 minutes; a list of points and combinations or a spreadsheet of location discrepancies takes up to 45. Validation and pre-filled fields could take over part of the lookup and checking; the change itself stays with the facilities team.

processes.description: Volume management and logistics staff find gas recorded at a meter with no valid deal or transport contract: a ticket has expired, flow began before a deal did, or old volumes sit in strangers gas. They ask the trader or desk for a spot, desk-to-desk or extended deal, or for approval to write the volume off to unaccounted-for gas. The trader creates or extends the ticket in Sitara and replies with the deal number; volume management applies, re-paths or brokers the volumes and sends the ticket back when its dates, price or counterparty are wrong.
steps: Volume management spots flow at a meter with no deal, an expired ticket or no contract while allocating volumes.
They check Sitara for the last deal ticket at the meter, its term and the contract tied to it.
They email the trader or desk with the meter, dates and volume, asking for a new or extended deal or a write-off approval.
The trader decides how the economics are handled and creates or extends the ticket, replying with the deal number.
Volume management checks the ticket's dates, price and counterparty and asks for a correction when it is wrong.
The volumes are applied, re-pathed or written off to unaccounted-for gas and the meter is cleared.

stalls.summary: Requests for a deal sit unanswered and have to be chased, leaving the flow unallocated until the trader replies.
Deals come back entered wrongly, with the wrong months or a price formula that has to be corrected, so the request goes round again.
Systems block the fix: a deal will not come across to Unify, a deal with an inactive or suspended counterparty cannot be extended, and flow does not carry over to mops.
Small volumes from flow recorded long before are left in strangers gas until logistics asks for a deal or for approval to write them off, so these problems stay open for a long time.

Requests reach the wrong person or miss people: an enquiry is first sent to someone who used to handle the work and then redirected, and a requester apologises for leaving a colleague off an earlier message.

contradictions.summary: The mail names different people as the one who sets up these deals: a counterparty and a sender citing Fred Boas point to Daren Farmer, while the same sender later says Danny Conner handles it.
A trader's pricing instruction for a new spot ticket was replaced by a different price formula in a follow-up, so the ticket had two conflicting instructions.
A deal cited to cover flow between ENA and HPL is contradicted by the reply that it is not a deal between those companies.

automation.approach: A daily exception report matching measured flow by meter against active deal tickets and transport contracts would list meters with flow and no valid deal, tickets nearing their end date, and counterparties that are inactive. Each exception would feed a standard request carrying the meter, dates, volume, last deal and contract to the trader, and small old volumes could be routed by rule to a write-off approval list.
automation.rationale: Most rounds start with a free-form note restating the same facts, and many come back wrong or unanswered. A standard request with the meter, dates, volume, counterparty, price basis and prior ticket gives traders what they need to enter the deal right the first time, and the report removes the manual search, while traders still decide the economics and enter the deals.

work_estimate.rationale: Per round, staff look up the meter's flow, the last deal ticket and the contract in Sitara, the trader creates or extends the ticket, and volume management checks it and re-applies, re-paths or writes off the volume. A simple extension takes about 10 minutes; a typical gap with a new ticket and re-allocation about 25; old strangers-gas cleanups and re-pathing up to 60. The search and matching are the automatable part; the deal decision and entry stay with people.

processes.description: A coordinator in logistics or accounting circulates the close schedule for the coming month, sometimes marked tentative and, at year-end, with its own dates, then sends a revised schedule after agreeing changes with other leads. Cut-offs are announced, such as a Friday evening after which no changes are allowed. During close, volume management reports which regions have flashed and asks groups to reply when their last-day file is complete, and accounting asks groups for their monthly submissions.
steps: The coordinator drafts the close calendar for the coming month from system and group deadlines.
The draft goes out as a tentative schedule to the logistics and accounting groups.
Leads discuss conflicts and a revised schedule is sent out.
The cut-off after which no changes are allowed is announced.
During close, groups report flash status and confirm when their last-day files are complete.
Accounting collects each group's monthly submissions.

stalls.summary: Schedules go out as tentative and are later reissued as revised after discussion among leads, so groups plan against dates that can move.

automation.approach: A close calendar generated from a standing layout of business-day rules for each system, with group deadlines filled in and a shared status tracker where each group marks its flash and last-day file as done, replacing the reply-when-complete requests.
automation.rationale: Each round rebuilds the same calendar and re-announces the same kinds of cut-offs. A template keeps the layout and rules fixed so only exceptions such as year-end or holidays need decisions, while leads still agree any revisions.

work_estimate.rationale: The hands-on work is drafting the calendar, checking it against system cut-offs and holidays, and reworking it after leads agree changes: about 30 minutes in a normal month, 15 when dates simply roll forward, and up to 60 at year-end or when the schedule is revised. A template could set most dates; agreeing the exceptions stays with people.
